incidents.title: Stolen admin token won't die
incidents.brief: An engineer's laptop was stolen at 09:40. Security clicked 'revoke session' at 10:02, yet admin calls from the laptop's token keep succeeding across all 40 services.
incidents.constraint: Revocation must take effect within minutes without a database read on every one of 90k req/s.
incidents.question: How do you make revocation stick?

choices.label: 10-minute access tokens plus a Redis jti denylist
choices.resultTitle: Stolen token dies in seconds
choices.resultBody: The token's jti goes into a Redis denylist checked in under 1 ms and its refresh token is revoked; entries only need to live 10 minutes, until the token expires anyway.

choices.label: Check every token against the sessions table on each request
choices.resultTitle: Postgres takes all 90k req/s
choices.resultBody: Revocation works, but 90k session reads a second push the users database past 95% CPU and checkout calls start timing out.

choices.label: Rotate the JWT signing key to kill the stolen token now
choices.resultTitle: Everyone logged out at once
choices.resultBody: A new signing key invalidates all 2M live tokens, not just the stolen one, so every user re-logs in and the login tier melts under 40k logins/s.

hints: A stateless token is valid until exp unless something says otherwise.
Shrink the window, then track only the few tokens revoked inside it.
Short access tokens plus refresh tokens, and a small denylist in Redis.

users: WAF: admin API calls from a new ASN, 14 per minute
UA curl/8.4 on /admin/* routes, token sub=admin-ekim
gw: INFO 90k req/s forwarded, Authorization header passed through
INFO /admin/* has no gateway policy; auth delegated to services
api: DEBUG jwt ok (local verify): sub=admin-ekim role=admin exp in 21h
db: 10:02 UPDATE sessions SET revoked_at=now() WHERE user='admin-ekim'

culprit.explanation: The 40 services check only the JWT's signature and exp locally and never consult revocation, so the revoked session row is never read. A 24-hour token lives 24 hours.

wrongNodeFeedback.users: The thief is the attacker, not the bug; you can't patch a stolen laptop. Ask why the system still accepts the token.
wrongNodeFeedback.db: The Users DB did record the revocation at 10:02; its logs show nobody ever reads it.
wrongNodeFeedback.gw: The gateway only passes the header through; the services are the ones saying yes.

incidents.title: Auth service called 360k times a second
incidents.brief: Auth service CPU hit 96% and API p95 is 640 ms, yet user traffic is flat at 30k req/s. Find out why auth is doing so much work.
incidents.constraint: Tokens are signed JWTs; logout must still take effect within 10 minutes.
incidents.question: How should services validate tokens?

choices.label: Cache introspection results per service for an hour
choices.resultTitle: Logouts lag by an hour
choices.resultBody: Auth CPU falls to 40%, but a revoked or logged-out token keeps working for up to 60 minutes in every service that cached it.

choices.label: Verify JWT signatures at the gateway with cached keys
choices.resultTitle: Auth leaves the hot path
choices.resultBody: The gateway checks signature and exp in about 50 µs with keys it already holds, so 360k introspection calls/s drop to zero and auth only serves logins and refreshes.

choices.label: Triple the auth service fleet behind its own balancer
choices.resultTitle: Bigger bill, same fan-out
choices.resultBody: Three times the auth servers absorb 360k calls/s for now, but every request still waits on 12 extra hops and auth stays a single point of failure.

hints: Does a signed token need a network call to be checked?
The public key is enough to verify a signature and exp.
Validate once at the edge; keep the auth service for logins.

users: RUM: API p95 640 ms, up from 90 ms
RUM: sessions and signups flat week over week
gw: INFO 30k req/s in, 30k out, flat week over week
svc: DEBUG orders: POST auth/introspect before every handler
DEBUG cart: POST auth/introspect before every handler
INFO shared auth middleware v3 rolled out to all 12 services
auth: WARN worker queue 4,200 deep, p95 610 ms

culprit.explanation: A shared middleware makes each of the 12 services call /introspect on every request, turning 30k user requests into 360k auth calls. The auth service is only the victim of that fan-out.

wrongNodeFeedback.auth: Auth is the loud victim: it's doing exactly the work it is asked. Ask who sends it 12x the user traffic.
wrongNodeFeedback.db: The token DB is busy because auth is busy; its queries are healthy.
wrongNodeFeedback.gw: The gateway passes through the same 30k req/s as last week.

incidents.title: Every new token rejected after rotation
incidents.brief: The identity provider rotated its signing key at 09:00. Gateways cache the JWKS for 24 h and don't know the new kid, so 100% of fresh tokens get 401.
incidents.constraint: The IdP's JWKS endpoint handles a few requests per minute, not per request.
incidents.question: What should the gateways do?

users: login at 09:04 succeeded at IdP, first API call returned 401
gw: jwks cache age 14 h of 24 h TTL
api: all requests carry a verified token header
idp: signing key rotated 09:00, new kid 'k-2026-10' published at /jwks

choices.label: Skip signature checks until the gateway caches expire
choices.resultTitle: Forged tokens accepted
choices.resultBody: The 401s stop, but for up to 24 hours a token with any signature passes, so anyone can mint an admin claim and walk in.

choices.label: Fetch the JWKS from the IdP on every single request
choices.resultTitle: Identity provider knocked over
choices.resultBody: 45k JWKS fetches a second hit an endpoint sized for a few a minute; it falls over and every validation and login fails with it.

choices.label: Refetch JWKS on an unknown kid, at most once a minute
choices.resultTitle: New kid learned in one fetch
choices.resultBody: The first token with the new kid triggers one JWKS fetch, the gateways learn the key and 401s stop within seconds, without hammering the IdP.

hints: The token's header says which key signed it.
An unknown kid means your key cache is stale, not that the token is forged.
Refresh keys on a kid miss, rate-limited; the IdP should publish new keys early.

incidents.title: Logins melt after a security tweak
incidents.brief: Security raised bcrypt cost from 10 to 14, so each hash takes 16x longer (~1 s of CPU). At the 09:00 peak of 800 logins/s, the auth pool sits at 99% and API calls time out.
incidents.constraint: Hashes must stay slow for attackers; API traffic must not share the login bottleneck.
incidents.question: What is the right fix?

users: API client timeout 5 s, retry storm
lb: upstream auth pool p95 4.2 s, 3.1k errors/min
login and API routes share one upstream pool
auth: bcrypt cost=14, about 1.0 s CPU per hash
API handlers queued behind hash jobs

choices.label: Switch to SHA-256, which hashes in microseconds
choices.resultTitle: Cracked at GPU speed
choices.resultBody: A GPU tries billions of SHA-256 guesses a second, so a leaked table of 8M accounts falls in hours; login CPU drops but the hashes protect nobody.

choices.label: Tune to cost 12 (~250 ms) on a separate login pool
choices.resultTitle: Slow for attackers, not for you
choices.resultBody: Cost 12 is 4x cheaper than 14 yet still ~250 ms per guess, and on its own pool a login burst no longer starves token refresh and API calls.

choices.label: Cache verified password hashes in Redis
choices.resultTitle: A fast oracle for every password
choices.resultBody: Logins get cheap, but Redis now holds a fast-to-check record of every recent password; one dump and attackers skip bcrypt entirely.

hints: Hashing should be slow per guess, but it only runs at login.
Pick a cost around 250 ms, not 1 s, and argon2id or bcrypt, never a fast hash.
Give password hashing its own capacity so it can't starve API traffic.

incidents.title: Credential stuffing under the limit
incidents.brief: 1.2M login attempts an hour arrive from 40k residential IPs, each trying once every 2 minutes. The 100/min per-IP limit never trips and 0.6% of attempts succeed.
incidents.constraint: Real users on shared office IPs must still log in without friction.
incidents.question: Which defense actually stops this?

choices.label: Cut the per-IP limit from 100 to 5 per minute
choices.resultTitle: Bots slip under, offices blocked
choices.resultBody: Each bot IP sends one attempt every 2 minutes, well under 5/min, while a 300-person office behind one NAT now gets 429s every morning.

choices.label: Lock any account after five failed login attempts
choices.resultTitle: Victims locked, attackers unfazed
choices.resultBody: Stuffing tries each leaked pair once, so valid pairs still succeed on the first attempt, and attackers can now lock out 50k real users on purpose.

choices.label: Challenge risky logins, reject breached passwords
choices.resultTitle: Stolen pairs stop working
choices.resultBody: New-device logins from high-failure IPs get a challenge and breached-password matches force a reset, so the 0.6% hit rate falls near zero while real users pass.

hints: Each IP and each account is barely used; what is unusual is the pattern.
The passwords come from other sites' breaches.
Score logins by device and failure rate, challenge the risky ones, check breach lists.

incidents.title: Fresh tokens 'not yet valid'
incidents.brief: After an autoscale, 6 of 40 new API nodes run 3 minutes slow because a firewall rule blocks NTP. Tokens issued seconds ago fail their nbf check there: 15% of requests get 401.
incidents.constraint: Access tokens live 10 minutes and must stay revocable.
incidents.question: How do you stop the random 401s?

choices.label: Retry every 401 once on a different API node
choices.resultTitle: The broken nodes stay hidden
choices.resultBody: Most retries land on a healthy node, but 6 of 40 nodes still reject fresh tokens, 401 traffic doubles and the clock fault is never fixed.

choices.label: Restore NTP on the new nodes and allow 60 s of leeway
choices.resultTitle: Clocks agree, tokens pass
choices.resultBody: The 6 drifted nodes resync to within milliseconds, and a 60-second leeway absorbs normal sub-second drift, so fresh tokens stop failing nbf checks.

choices.label: Raise access token lifetime from 10 minutes to 24 hours
choices.resultTitle: Still not valid, now less revocable
choices.resultBody: The token's nbf is still 3 minutes ahead of the drifted clocks, so the 401s continue, and a stolen token now stays usable for a whole day.

hints: Only the new nodes reject tokens. What differs about them?
exp, nbf and iat are compared against the local clock.
Fix time sync, and allow a small leeway for normal drift.

incidents.title: Token refreshes fail on long-lived signer pods
incidents.brief: Since an HSM client SDK upgrade, Keyring's token-signer pods leak file descriptors. After about 20 hours a pod hits its 65k limit, and 1 in 6 token refreshes fails.
incidents.constraint: The vendor's patched SDK ships Friday, and access tokens must stay at 10 minutes.
incidents.question: What keeps refreshes working until Friday?

choices.label: Extend access tokens from 10 minutes to 12 hours
choices.resultTitle: Refreshes recover, holding for now
choices.resultBody: Signings drop 72x, so refresh failures fall to 2% and descriptors creep up slowly. Access tokens now stay valid for 12 hours, and nothing checks them before expiry.

choices.label: Rolling restart of token-signer pods every 12 hours

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A temporary scheduled restart that must be deleted when the patched SDK lands.

choices.resultTitle: No pod lives long enough to leak out
choices.resultBody: A scheduled rollout replaces one signer pod at a time every 12 hours, so descriptors peak near 40k and never reach the limit; failed refreshes fall to 0.05%. Cost: each new pod spends ~2 s opening HSM sessions before it is ready.

choices.label: Move signing into a new dedicated signing microservice
choices.resultTitle: Two sprints later, the same leak
choices.resultBody: Building the service takes two sprints, refreshes keep failing until it ships, and it links the same HSM SDK, so its pods leak descriptors and hit the 65k limit the same way.

hints: CPU and latency look normal; count something else on the signer.
The descriptor count starts near zero every time a pod starts.
Friday is close; you only need to keep any pod from reaching 20 hours of uptime.

incidents.title: Offboarded contractor's token still works
incidents.brief: The 12-hour tokens kept refreshes up. HR offboarded a contractor at 09:00; at 11:30 their token is still exporting customer lists, because no service checks a token before its 12-hour expiry.
incidents.constraint: The signer's descriptor-leak fix still ships Friday.
incidents.question: What kills the token now and restores the 10-minute promise?

choices.label: Denylist its jti, then restore 10-minute tokens with signer restarts
choices.resultTitle: Token dead in seconds, promise restored
choices.resultBody: The contractor's jti goes into a Redis denylist and their next call gets 401; access tokens return to 10 minutes, and 12-hourly signer restarts keep descriptors well under 65k until Friday.

choices.label: Rotate the JWT signing key so the contractor's token dies
choices.resultTitle: Everyone logged out, signer overwhelmed
choices.resultBody: All 2M live tokens die at once, not just the contractor's; the leaking signer pods must mint 2M new tokens in minutes, hit 65k descriptors, and 70% of refreshes fail.

choices.label: Delete the contractor's account and sessions from the Users DB
choices.resultTitle: The token never asks the database
choices.resultBody: Services verify the JWT locally and never read the account row, so the contractor's token keeps working until 21:00, and the audit log shows exports after the deletion.

hints: A signed token is valid until exp unless something says otherwise.
Deleting data the services never read changes nothing.
Kill this one token, then shrink the window back.

incidents.title: Token refresh storm every ten minutes
incidents.brief: Switching to 10-minute tokens re-logged all 2M users at 10:05, so their tokens expire together. Every ten minutes 2M refreshes land within 30 s and the token service melts.
incidents.constraint: Access tokens must stay at 10 minutes for revocation.
incidents.question: How do refreshes stop arriving all at once?

choices.label: Refresh at a random point in the token's last 30% of life
choices.resultTitle: Refreshes spread across the window
choices.resultBody: Each client now refreshes somewhere between minute 7 and 10, so 2M refreshes spread over 3 minutes: about 11k a second instead of 66k, and token-service CPU settles near 55%.

choices.label: Extend access tokens back to 24 hours to thin out refreshes
choices.resultTitle: Refreshes vanish, so does revocation
choices.resultBody: Refreshes almost disappear, but a revoked token lives a day again, undoing the fix for the stolen admin token, and the next forced re-login syncs every client again.

choices.label: Keep the token service at 20x its usual size for the peaks
choices.resultTitle: Paying for 30 seconds in ten minutes
choices.resultBody: Twenty times the pods absorb each 30 s spike, but they idle 95% of every ten minutes, adding about $6k a month, and the peaks grow with every new user.

nodes.sub: x20 pods, idle 95% of the time

hints: The tokens were all born in the same minute.
Every client refreshes at exactly the same age.
Add randomness to when each client refreshes.

incidents.title: One carrier's users hit a CAPTCHA every login
incidents.brief: Risk challenges stopped the stuffing, but a big carrier's CGNAT puts 400k real customers behind 900 IPs that also carried bots. They now get a CAPTCHA every login; 1 in 5 give up.
incidents.constraint: The botnet is still probing from residential and mobile IPs.
incidents.question: How do real users on shared IPs stop being challenged?

choices.label: Let signed trusted-device cookies skip the login challenge
choices.resultTitle: Known phones sail through
choices.resultBody: After one good login a device gets a signed per-device cookie the risk engine trusts, so 95% of returning carrier users skip the CAPTCHA while bots without one are still challenged.

choices.label: Allowlist the carrier's 900 IP addresses in the risk engine
choices.resultTitle: Bots ride the same carrier
choices.resultBody: Carrier users sail through, and so do the bots renting mobile proxies on that carrier; successful stuffing logins climb back to 0.4% within a day.

choices.label: Raise the risk threshold so far fewer logins get challenged
choices.resultTitle: Everyone challenged less, bots too
choices.resultBody: Challenges drop for everyone, including the botnet; stuffing successes rise to 0.3% while carrier users behind the worst-scored IPs still see a CAPTCHA.

hints: The IP is shared by real users and bots, so it can't tell them apart.
A returning user's device is stronger evidence than the IP.
Remember devices that already passed a login.

incidents.title: JWKS cache miss stampede during token signing key rotation
incidents.brief: When an identity provider rotates its RSA signing key, 200 microservices simultaneously fetch the new `.well-known/jwks.json`, taking down the auth server.
incidents.constraint: Enable seamless key rotation without dogpiling the JWKS authorization endpoint.
incidents.question: How should JWKS caching and key rollover be orchestrated across microservices?

choices.label: Pre-publish new keys 24h ahead and cache JWKS with stale-while-revalidate
choices.resultTitle: Key pre-publishing eliminated rotation stampedes
choices.resultBody: Publishing the upcoming public key before using it to sign tokens ensures microservice JWKS caches already have the key when new tokens land.

choices.label: Disable JWKS local caching so every microservice fetches keys per request
choices.resultTitle: Disabling caching paralyzed all microservice communications
choices.resultBody: Making 46,000 HTTP calls per second to fetch JWKS keys crushed the identity provider and added hundreds of milliseconds of latency.

choices.label: Stop rotating signing keys and use a permanent hardcoded RSA key pair
choices.resultTitle: Never rotating keys violated security compliance mandates
choices.resultBody: Static signing keys violate SOC2 and PCI-DSS compliance requirements and leave the system defenseless if a private key leaks.

hints: JWKS files contain public keys identified by a Key ID (`kid`).
During rotation, the identity provider should add the new key to JWKS hours before signing tokens with it.
`stale-while-revalidate` serves cached keys immediately while refreshing in the background.

incidents.title: Synchronous token revocation check saturates central Redis master
incidents.brief: Checking a central Redis token revocation blocklist on every API request consumes 85,000 queries/second, bottlenecking cluster throughput.
incidents.constraint: Verify revocations within 60 seconds without querying a central database per request.
incidents.question: How should token revocation checks be decoupled for high throughput?

choices.label: Issue short 5-minute JWTs and broadcast revocation Bloom filters to edge
choices.resultTitle: Short JWTs and edge Bloom filters eliminated Redis bottlenecks
choices.resultBody: Short-lived tokens expire naturally in 5 minutes; explicit revocations are broadcast to in-memory edge Bloom filters with zero database queries.

choices.label: Increase Redis client connection pool to 5,000 connections per gateway
choices.resultTitle: Massive connection pool crashed Redis with memory exhaustion
choices.resultBody: Opening thousands of concurrent TCP sockets to a single-threaded Redis process multiplied context switching and crashed Redis.

choices.label: Disable token revocation entirely and issue non-expiring 10-year tokens
choices.resultTitle: Non-expiring tokens made stolen user credentials permanent
choices.resultBody: Stolen user tokens could never be invalidated, leaving hacked user accounts vulnerable to unauthorized account takeover.

hints: Stateless JWTs cannot be revoked without state storage or short expiration windows.
Short token expiry (e.g. 5–15 minutes) limits the window of vulnerability automatically.
Bloom filters or local caches updated via pub/sub let gateways check revocations in memory.

incidents.title: Bloated JWT claim payload triggers HTTP 431 header overflow
incidents.brief: Teams pack user permissions, roles, and org hierarchies into JWT tokens, inflating token size to 12KB and causing upstream NGINX proxies to reject requests.
incidents.constraint: Ensure requests pass HTTP header limits (<4KB) while maintaining role authorization.
incidents.question: How should JWT claim payloads be designed for scale?

choices.label: Emit lean JWTs with subject ID and tenant ID, fetching roles on gateway cache
choices.resultTitle: Lean JWT tokens resolved header size overflow cleanly
choices.resultBody: Keeping JWTs small (<1KB) avoids proxy buffer limits; granular permission sets are resolved and cached on internal gateway tiers.

choices.label: Increase NGINX large_client_header_buffers to 64k across all proxies
choices.resultTitle: Inflated header buffers doubled proxy memory footprints
choices.resultBody: Allocating 64KB buffers per connection bloated proxy memory and failed whenever third-party CDNs or mobile clients enforced strict limits.

choices.label: Convert all HTTP GET requests to POST so tokens travel inside JSON bodies
choices.resultTitle: Converting GET to POST broke browser caching and CDN edge routing
choices.resultBody: Using POST bodies for read queries destroyed HTTP caching, broke RESTful conventions, and increased latency across client devices.

hints: JWTs travel on every single HTTP request in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header.
Most CDNs, reverse proxies, and browsers cap headers at 4KB to 8KB.
Tokens should contain identity claims (sub, iss, exp), not thousands of fine-grained permissions.

variants.constraint: Tokens only cross our own NGINX tier, never a CDN or browser. The factory controllers downstream authorize offline, so roles must travel inside the token.

auth-09-raise-proxy-buffers.resultTitle: Headers fit, roles stay in the token
auth-09-raise-proxy-buffers.resultBody: With 64k header buffers, the 12 KB tokens pass NGINX and the offline controllers keep every role claim. NGINX allocates large buffers only for big headers, so memory rises modestly: about $75 a month across the proxies.

auth-09-trim-claims.resultBody: Lean tokens pass the proxies, but the factory controllers have no network path to a role service. Every request arrives with only sub and tenant, and the controllers deny it: the 431s become 403s.

hints: Where are these tokens read, and can those readers look anything up?
The 4 KB limit belongs to CDNs and browsers, and neither is in this path.
When every hop is yours, the header limit is a setting, not a law.

incidents.title: Intensive RSA signature verification saturates gateway CPU
incidents.brief: An API Gateway verifying RSA-4096 JWT signatures across 75,000 req/s burns 95% CPU solely evaluating modular exponentiation math.
incidents.constraint: Verify asymmetric cryptographic signatures at high throughput without saturating CPU.
incidents.question: Which cryptographic algorithm provides fast verification for high-throughput tokens?

choices.label: Migrate token signing algorithm to Ed25519 (EdDSA) or ECDSA P-256
choices.resultTitle: Elliptic curve verification reduced CPU consumption by 80%
choices.resultBody: Ed25519 provides equivalent 128-bit cryptographic security with signature verification speeds roughly 5x faster than RSA.

choices.label: Inspect JWT claims by decoding base64 without verifying the signature
choices.resultTitle: Skipping verification allowed complete authentication bypass
choices.resultBody: Failing to verify the signature allowed malicious attackers to forge arbitrary user and admin roles in base64 payloads.

choices.label: Scale out API gateway fleet to 60 instances running high-CPU servers
choices.resultTitle: Brute-force server scaling inflated infrastructure spend
choices.resultBody: Scaling up dozens of expensive servers to perform inefficient RSA math wasted budget without solving the algorithmic bottleneck.

hints: RSA-4096 requires intensive modular exponentiation calculations.
Elliptic curve algorithms (EdDSA / Ed25519 or ES256) offer smaller key sizes and vastly faster signature computation.
Never skip signature verification in production.

variants.constraint: 2M smart meters verify these tokens with firmware that supports only RSA, and a firmware rollout takes 18 months. Finance has approved $600 a month for gateway capacity.

auth-10-scale-gateway.resultTitle: Brute force is the honest answer
auth-10-scale-gateway.resultBody: Sixty high-CPU instances spread the RSA-4096 verification until CPU sits near 55%, and the meters keep working. It costs $600 a month for 18 months; plan the move to Ed25519 alongside the next firmware.

auth-10-migrate-eddsa.resultTitle: Meters can't verify the new signatures
auth-10-migrate-eddsa.resultBody: Gateway CPU drops, but Ed25519-signed tokens fail on 2M meters whose firmware knows only RSA. Every meter rejects its token and stops reporting until an 18-month firmware rollout lands.

hints: Who else has to verify these signatures besides the gateway?
The algorithm is fixed for 18 months by devices you can't update.
If the math per request can't shrink, the capacity must grow.

incidents.title: OAuth2 token introspection latency spikes downstream service call chain
incidents.brief: Microservices validate opaque bearer tokens by calling the OAuth2 `/oauth/introspect` endpoint synchronously, adding 45ms to every internal RPC call.
incidents.constraint: Eliminate network hops for internal token verification while preserving auth integrity.
incidents.question: How should authentication tokens be validated across internal microservices?

choices.label: Verify token once at gateway and pass short-lived signed internal JWTs
choices.resultTitle: Edge token translation eliminated internal introspection hops
choices.resultBody: The API gateway validates external tokens and mints a short-lived internal JWT, allowing downstream services to verify claims cryptographically.

choices.label: Cache introspection responses in memory on every service for 2 hours
choices.resultTitle: 2-hour local caching allowed revoked tokens to access sensitive APIs
choices.resultBody: Caching introspection responses for 2 hours meant revoked user sessions continued to make unauthorized calls across microservices.

choices.label: Remove user tokens entirely and trust all internal traffic via mutual TLS
choices.resultTitle: Removing user tokens eliminated end-user auditability
choices.resultBody: Relying purely on mTLS identifies the calling service but loses the authenticated user identity, breaking authorization and audit logs.

hints: Opaque tokens require remote network introspection (RFC 7662) to discover token validity.
Calling introspection from dozens of microservices multiplies RPC hops and latency.
The 'Token Exchange / Gateway Translation' pattern translates opaque tokens into signed internal JWTs.

variants.constraint: Half of all calls reach services straight from partner VPCs, bypassing the gateway. The IdP has no revocation: tokens only die at their 2-hour expiry.

auth-11-cache-introspect.resultTitle: Cached answers can't go stale here
auth-11-cache-introspect.resultBody: Each service introspects a token once and caches the answer until the token expires. With no revocation, a cached 'active' can't become wrong, so the 45 ms hop drops out of about 99% of calls, gateway or not.

auth-11-gateway-translation.resultTitle: Half the traffic skips the gateway
auth-11-gateway-translation.resultBody: Internal JWTs fix calls that enter through the gateway, but partner calls from their VPCs never touch it. Those services still introspect every request, so half the traffic keeps its 45 ms hop and the IdP stays hot.

hints: Which requests never pass through the gateway?
Without revocation, can a token's validity change before it expires?
An answer that can't change is safe to remember until it expires.

incidents.title: Login p99 goes from 90 ms to 3.4 s and the auth DB is at 96% CPU
incidents.brief: The session DB now takes 41k lookups a second, up from 3k, while API traffic is flat at 41k req/s. Auth service CPU is only 45%. Three PRs shipped at 09:40; login failures are rising.
incidents.constraint: Users are locked out; one revert must fit in the next deploy.
incidents.question: Which PR do you revert to bring the auth DB back down?

choices.label: Revert PR #6120: gateway JWT verify to remote introspection
choices.diff:
gateway/authz.yaml
-  mode: jwt_local_verify
+  mode: introspect_remote
+  introspection_cache_ttl: 0s
   jwks_refresh: 10m
choices.resultTitle: Signatures verified in the gateway again
choices.resultBody: Remote introspection sends every API request to the auth DB: 41k lookups a second, up 14x from the 3k that logins and refreshes cause. Verifying JWT signatures locally with cached keys removes those lookups; DB CPU falls to 12% and login p99 to 85 ms. Cost: a revoked token stays valid until it expires.

choices.label: Revert PR #6133: bcrypt cost from 10 to 12 on password login
choices.diff:
auth/password.go
-const bcryptCost = 12
+const bcryptCost = 10
 // constant applies to new hashes
choices.resultTitle: Login hashing is not the bottleneck
choices.resultBody: Cost 12 makes each hash about 4x slower (roughly 250 ms), but logins are only 300 a second and that CPU lives on the auth pods, which are at 45%. The DB stays at 95% with 41k lookups a second and p99 hardly moves.

choices.label: Revert PR #6141: access token lifetime from 5 minutes to 15
choices.resultTitle: Refresh traffic was never the load
choices.resultBody: Token lifetime changes how often clients refresh: at 5 minutes that is well under 1k refreshes a second. Restoring 15 minutes cuts them a little but the 41k per-request lookups remain; DB CPU stays 94% and p99 is 3.1 s.

hints: API traffic is flat but DB lookups grew 14x.
Something now hits the DB on every request instead of every login.
Which diff changes how a token is validated at the gateway?

incidents.title: Auth stack costs $26,000 a month while running at 15% CPU
incidents.brief: Twelve auth pods handle 9k req/s at 15% CPU and p95 45 ms. A Redis revocation list uses 22% of memory, and a standby cluster in region B takes 0% traffic. Finance asks for a cut.
incidents.constraint: Revoked tokens must stop working within 60 s and a region loss must recover in under 5 minutes.
incidents.question: Which cut saves money without breaking the SLO?

choices.label: Remove the standby cluster in region B that takes no traffic
choices.resultTitle: No region to fail over to
choices.resultBody: The standby's 0% utilisation is exactly what a warm spare looks like. Without it a region A outage means logins are down until a cluster is rebuilt, around 40 minutes, against the 5 minute recovery objective.

choices.label: Drop the revocation list and rely on 15-minute token expiry
choices.resultTitle: Revoked tokens live for 15 minutes
choices.resultBody: The list is small and cheap, but it is how a stolen or logged-out token dies quickly. Without it a revoked token keeps working until it expires, up to 15 minutes, against the 60 second requirement.

choices.label: Cut auth pods in region A from 12 to 6, about 30% CPU each
choices.resultTitle: Half the pods carry the same traffic
choices.resultBody: At 15% CPU, twelve pods do 1.8 pods' worth of work. On six that is 30% CPU, and losing one pod leaves 36%. p95 goes from 45 to 52 ms, far inside SLO. The bill falls by roughly $2,600. Cost: less headroom for a 3x login spike before autoscaling reacts.

hints: Low utilisation is only a saving when nothing depends on the idle part.
Match each idle component to the requirement it protects.
Which capacity is over-provisioned without backing a revocation or recovery promise?

incidents.title: Users logged out in waves every minute
incidents.brief: AcmeID has 600,000 concurrent sessions on 1-minute access tokens. Every client refreshes each minute: 10,000 refreshes/s against an IdP sized for 3,000/s, so refreshes fail with 429 and sessions drop.
incidents.constraint: Compliance needs a revoked or fired user's access to end within 15 minutes.
incidents.question: What access-token lifetime keeps the IdP alive and revocation inside 15 minutes?

choices.label: Issue 5-15 minute access tokens with rotating refresh tokens
choices.resultTitle: Refreshes fit the IdP
choices.resultBody: A 10-minute lifetime cuts refreshes to 1,000/s, a third of IdP capacity, and revocation takes effect within 10 minutes. Cost: a stolen access token stays usable for up to 10 minutes, and refresh-token rotation adds a store to maintain.

choices.label: Keep 1-minute tokens and double the identity provider fleet
choices.resultTitle: Still short of 10k a second
choices.resultBody: Doubling the fleet lifts capacity to 6,000 refreshes/s against 10,000 needed, so 40% of refreshes still fail, and the bill rises about $3,200 a month to burn CPU on re-signing tokens every minute.

choices.label: Issue 8-hour tokens and sweep a revocation list nightly
choices.resultTitle: Fired staff keep access for hours
choices.resultBody: Refreshes drop to 21/s, but a revoked user's token works for up to 8 hours and the nightly sweep leaves a gap of up to 24, so every revocation breaks the 15-minute rule.

nodes.sub: 8 h tokens, revocation gap up to 24 h

hints: Refresh load is sessions divided by token lifetime.
Revocation can only take effect when the access token expires.
Pick a lifetime where load fits the IdP and the revocation window fits compliance.

knob.label: Access-token lifetime
knob.question: Set the lifetime so refreshes fit the IdP and revocation stays inside 15 minutes.

low.title: IdP drowns in refreshes
low.body: At 3 minutes or less 600,000 sessions refresh 3,300 to 10,000 times a second against a 3,000/s IdP, so refreshes return 429 and sessions drop.

high.title: Revocation takes too long
high.body: At 30 minutes a fired user's access token stays valid for up to 30 minutes, twice the 15-minute compliance limit, even though the IdP sits near idle.

good.title: Load fits, revocation fits
good.body: At 5 to 15 minutes refreshes run at 667 to 2,000 per second, under the 3,000/s capacity, and revoked access ends within 15 minutes.

incidents.title: Signing key pasted in a public repo
incidents.brief: A contractor pushed the IdP's RS256 private key (kid k-07) to a public repo 20 minutes ago. Gateways still trust it, and forged admin tokens reach the API about 1,900 times a minute.
incidents.constraint: 400,000 real users hold live tokens signed with k-07, and the login pool handles 800 logins/s.
incidents.question: Gateways now reject k-07 and 400,000 users get 401. How do you get them back safely?

users: admin API calls from 14 new IPs using kid k-07
gw: 1,900 admin-scope tokens/min from IPs never seen before
api: POST /admin/users/export 412 times in 10 min from 14 IPs
authz ok: scope admin, issuer idp
idp: audit: no admin logins match these tokens, no password events

choices.label: Let clients swap refresh tokens for new-key access tokens
choices.resultTitle: Sessions recover without passwords
choices.resultBody: Clients present refresh tokens, which are opaque and were never signed with k-07, and receive access tokens signed by the new key; 400,000 sessions recover in about 4 minutes at 1,700 refreshes/s. Cost: any refresh token that leaked too must be revoked separately.

choices.label: Re-accept k-07 only for tokens whose iat predates the leak
choices.resultTitle: Attackers backdate iat
choices.resultBody: The iat claim is written by whoever signs the token, and the attacker holds the key, so a forged token with yesterday's iat passes the check and forgeries resume at 1,900 a minute.

choices.label: Force every user through password plus MFA login again
choices.resultTitle: Login pool melts
choices.resultBody: 400,000 logins against a pool that handles 800/s take at least 8 minutes, bcrypt CPU pins at 99%, and every user gets an MFA prompt at once; p95 reaches 4 s and support is flooded.

hints: The forged tokens need the key, not a password.
Anything inside a token can be written by whoever holds the signing key.
A credential that was never signed with the leaked key can be exchanged for a fresh one.

mitigation.question: Forged admin tokens are being accepted right now. What is the first move?

choices.label: Publish a new key and remove k-07 from the JWKS
choices.resultTitle: Forgeries stop at the gateway
choices.resultBody: Within one JWKS refresh of about 60 s every token signed with k-07 fails verification, so forged tokens drop from 1,900 a minute to 0. Cost: all 400,000 genuine tokens signed with k-07 fail too, and users see 401 until they get new ones.

choices.label: Cut access-token lifetime from 15 minutes to 5 minutes
choices.resultTitle: The attacker writes the expiry
choices.resultBody: Forged tokens carry whatever exp the attacker signs, so a shorter default lifetime in the IdP changes nothing and they keep verifying at 1,900 a minute.

choices.label: Force a password reset for all 2,000 admin accounts
choices.resultTitle: Passwords were never the way in
choices.resultBody: Forging a token needs the signing key, not a password, so the reset floods support with 600 tickets while forged tokens still verify at 1,900 a minute.
